01-feature-building.notes: All ten pass the hidden contract tests and match a brute-force greedy reference on 1,500 random DAGs and 500 random cyclic graphs. The real differences come from targeted probes. I raises RecursionError on cycles of 2,000 or more nodes. F rejects whitespace-only IDs, which the contract allows. H takes 16 s on 20k jobs. G drops dependencies given as a one-shot iterator. A, E and I leak TypeError for depends_on=None. Most cross-test failures are stricter than the contract: exact message wording, extra type validation (non-Job items, priority types), or a choice between listing downstream blocked jobs and only cycle members. These were not counted against contract correctness. Cross-test failures that do show contract problems: F rejecting ' ' (fails A, B and E suites) and I's recursion on long cycles (fails D, F, J and B suites). G's float-priority rejection is defensible given the int type hint and was penalized lightly. Test quality was measured with 25 wrapper mutants: each wraps the suite's own implementation, so wording expectations still pass, and injects one bug (FIFO ready queue, tie by ID, priority inheritance, recursive cycle detection, ignoring unknown dependencies, input mutation, and others). Unmutated baseline: all suites pass. B, D and J are tied at 10; D is ranked first for its exact cycle path plus blocked count and its reported extra fuzzing, then B for exact SCC membership. H and F are tied at 8.25; H ranks higher because it is contract-correct but slow, while F rejects valid input.
